paras: The burning of Floyd King's house was a suspected arson in early March 1882 in which the house of Floyd King, a Black man, was burned in Oconee, apparently Oconee County, Georgia. Two white tramps were thought to be responsible, but no arrest was reported, and the burning is known only from one short paragraph in the Savannah Morning News.

The Savannah Morning News described King as "an industrious colored man, who accumulated some $5,000 since the war." The paragraph gives no further detail about his property, his household or his standing among his neighbors.

King's house was burned at night "a few nights ago," counting from the report of March 11, 1882. Suspicion fell on two white tramps, because they had been "seen hanging around the neighborhood" before the fire. The next morning two tracks were found around the building, which the paper took as support for that suspicion. No one is reported to have been hurt, and the item gives no suspect's name and no motive.
No report of an arrest, an inquiry or any official response appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News ran the item on March 11, 1882, as a single uncredited paragraph in a front-page column of Georgia news. In the same column it sat between a Newnan elopement and a child revived after nearly drowning in Oglethorpe, with no headline and no comment of its own. The paper framed the attribution to the tramps as a suspicion ("It is thought"), identified King as "colored," and noted his savings without tying them to the fire. No other report of the burning, in the white or the Black press, appears in the coverage.
